Apex InsightSeptember 5, 2026

The Shock Has Moved Outside Labor

Payrolls have stabilized enough to reduce near-term recession risk, but oil, term premium, and long-end yields are now setting the policy problem.

Key Conclusions

  • Oil is increasingly connecting geopolitical risk to inflation uncertainty, term premium, and long-term financing costs, making crude as important as labor data for the fall setup.
  • Treasury futures shorts can amplify rallies, but the persistence of high yields after some short covering argues positioning is not the whole story.
  • Labor-market churn and wage pressure remain subdued, so the domestic wage mechanism is cooling even as the Fed faces another headline inflation impulse.
  • August payrolls reduced imminent recession risk, while diffusion and temporary help suggest early cyclical stabilization without proving broad hiring reacceleration.
Opening Argument

The Shock Has Moved Outside Labor

The macro debate has shifted again. Only a few weeks ago, the primary question was whether deterioration in the labor market would force policymakers to become more patient. Today, the more important question is whether enough of that downside risk has receded for the Federal Reserve to respond more aggressively to an inflation problem increasingly being shaped outside the labor market. That distinction matters because the forces determining inflation, interest rates, and employment are no longer moving together as cleanly as they did earlier in the cycle.

The economy is entering the fall with an unusual combination of resilient activity and increasingly restrictive market-based financial conditions. The employment backdrop has stabilized enough to reduce immediate recession concerns, but worker mobility remains subdued and wage pressures continue moderating. At the same time, geopolitical developments are influencing energy prices and the long end of the Treasury curve more directly, creating an inflation impulse that monetary policy has limited ability to solve without imposing additional restraint elsewhere.

This leaves the Fed confronting a different problem than the one that defined much of the post-pandemic tightening cycle. The question is no longer simply whether excessive labor demand requires higher rates. It is whether policymakers should tighten against persistent inflation when the domestic wage mechanism is already cooling, particularly when the same inflation shock is independently pushing long-term borrowing costs higher. With September seasonality becoming less favorable for risk assets and Treasury positioning capable of amplifying moves in either direction, the interaction between oil, rates, and the Fed's reaction function has become the more important variable to watch.

Oil And Duration

Crude Is Repricing the Long End

For much of the past several years, the labor market was one of the dominant drivers of Treasury yields. Economic surprises around payrolls, unemployment, wages, and broader labor conditions translated relatively cleanly into changes in the expected path of Fed policy, giving labor data a strong directional relationship with rates. Since the beginning of the Iran conflict, however, that relationship has become considerably less important. The marginal driver of the long end increasingly looks like oil, inflation uncertainty, and the geopolitical risk surrounding the conflict rather than incremental changes in employment.

The chart below captures that transition. The 10-year Treasury yield has moved increasingly closely with WTI crude, with the rolling 30-day correlation of daily changes now around 0.66. WTI is back near $91 while the 10-year has pushed toward 4.79%, and the two have increasingly moved together as the conflict has persisted. Oil is not mechanically determining the level of Treasury yields, but it has become an important transmission mechanism connecting the geopolitical shock to inflation expectations, Fed policy, nominal growth, and ultimately the compensation investors demand for holding duration.

That last point is particularly important. Decomposing the long end into expected short rates and term premium shows that today's move cannot simply be explained by investors pricing a higher Fed Funds rate. Term premium has risen materially as well, reflecting the additional compensation investors require for accepting uncertainty over inflation, fiscal sustainability, Treasury supply, and the future path of rates. We have discussed the fiscal component extensively throughout our research, with persistent deficits and enormous financing requirements already creating a structural reason for investors to demand greater compensation for holding duration. The Iran conflict and renewed oil shock have effectively added another layer of uncertainty on top of that existing problem.

Oil matters to term premium because investors care not only about the expected level of inflation but also the uncertainty surrounding that outcome. A persistent geopolitical shock capable of moving crude between $70 and $100+ creates a wider distribution around future inflation, nominal growth, and Fed policy. Even if policymakers ultimately look through the first-round impact of higher gasoline prices, investors holding a 10- or 30-year Treasury still need to price the possibility that the shock lasts longer, feeds into transportation and production costs, changes inflation expectations, or eventually migrates into underlying inflation.

This is also why the increase in long yields matters more to the real economy than the debate surrounding the next 25 basis point move in Fed Funds alone. The 10-year Treasury sits much closer to the financing mechanism for mortgages, corporate borrowing, commercial real estate, and other long-duration investment decisions. We have already seen the consequences in housing, where elevated mortgage rates continue suppressing turnover and residential construction. If oil keeps the long end elevated through higher inflation expectations and term premium, financial conditions can continue tightening even without another formal Fed hike.

The complication is that the oil shock is simultaneously pushing the FOMC toward a more hawkish reaction function. Governor Michael Barr's recent comments fit directly with the framework Kevin Warsh outlined at Jackson Hole. Barr characterized the labor market as stable, unemployment as relatively low, economic growth as solid, and consumer spending as resilient, while also highlighting the contribution from AI-related business investment. Against that backdrop, inflation remaining above target for more than five years has made policymakers increasingly reluctant to simply assume another supply shock will disappear on its own.

Barr's policy standard was explicit. If incoming data provide confidence that inflation is moving sustainably toward 2%, the Fed has time to remain patient. If inflation fails to moderate sufficiently, he argued policymakers should be prepared to raise rates decisively. That leaves September as a genuinely live meeting because the FOMC increasingly views the cost of allowing another inflation impulse to become embedded as potentially greater than the cost of additional restraint while employment and aggregate demand remain resilient.

The problem is that higher policy rates cannot resolve the source of the current shock. Another hike does not produce additional barrels of oil, resolve the Iran conflict, or eliminate the fiscal risk premium embedded in long-duration Treasuries. It would instead tighten financial conditions most aggressively across the portions of the economy already struggling with elevated borrowing costs. Housing, small businesses, and lower-income consumers would absorb additional restraint even though they are not responsible for the supply constraint generating the initial inflation pressure.

There is nevertheless a credibility argument for tightening. After more than five years of above-target inflation, the FOMC increasingly appears unwilling to treat every new inflation shock as temporary. A hike could reinforce the Fed's commitment to price stability and potentially contain longer-term inflation expectations. In the best case, greater credibility at the front end could even relieve some pressure on term premium farther out the curve. The risk is that policymakers tighten into a supply shock while the bond market continues demanding greater compensation for fiscal and geopolitical uncertainty anyway, leaving both the policy rate and long-term market rates restrictive simultaneously.

That combination becomes more important as we enter a seasonally less forgiving period for equities. September has historically produced weaker equity returns and rising volatility into the fall, and the current market is entering that window with several macro pressure points already in place. Long yields are rising, oil is moving higher, the Fed retains tightening optionality, and geopolitical uncertainty remains elevated. In a midterm election year, the fall calendar also introduces another potential source of headline and policy volatility.

Market breadth has already begun reflecting some of that pressure. The percentage of S&P 500 constituents trading above their 20-day moving averages has fallen sharply to roughly 35% from 68% only a few weeks ago. Longer-term breadth remains considerably healthier, with more than 68% of members still above their 200-day moving averages, so the deterioration should not yet be interpreted as a structural breakdown in the bull market. The distinction is that short-term participation is weakening well before the long-term trend has broken.

That makes the current setup increasingly dependent on whether the oil-yield feedback loop stabilizes. If crude rolls over, inflation pressure eases, and the 10-year retreats, the Fed receives additional room to remain patient while equity breadth can repair without significant index-level damage. If WTI continues higher, however, the same shock simultaneously raises headline inflation, reinforces the FOMC's tightening bias, pressures term premium, and keeps long-term financing costs elevated.

For much of this cycle, investors could look to the labor market to understand where yields were headed next. The chart below suggests the marginal variable has changed. Oil has increasingly become the bridge between geopolitics, inflation, Fed policy, term premium, and financial conditions. With its 30-day correlation to the 10-year now above 0.60, the path of crude may matter as much as the next payroll report for determining whether the fall begins with a routine increase in volatility or something more consequential.

Treasury Positioning

Shorts Are Fuel, Not the Whole Story

The positioning data add an important layer to the oil and Treasury relationship discussed above. Rising crude, persistent inflation uncertainty, and higher term premium are increasingly providing a fundamental reason for long-end yields to remain elevated, but speculative positioning can amplify the move in either direction. CFTC data continue to show historically large net short exposure across Treasury futures, with the legacy non-commercial series shown below at roughly 883K contracts net short in the 2-year and 909K net short in the 10-year. In the more granular positioning data, leveraged funds remain roughly 2.13 million contracts net short the 10-year while asset managers hold approximately 2.59 million contracts net long.

Those numbers require some qualification because Treasury futures positioning is not equivalent to a simple directional bet on rates. A meaningful portion of leveraged-fund shorts reflects basis trades and other relative-value strategies where futures exposure is offset by positions elsewhere in the Treasury market. Asset-manager longs can similarly reflect hedging and duration-management activity. The gross positioning therefore cannot simply be interpreted as hedge funds betting that yields rise while traditional managers bet that yields fall.

The change in positioning is nevertheless informative. Leveraged funds covered roughly 95K net short contracts over the latest week, yet the 10-year yield remains near 4.8%. That matters because if the rise in yields were predominantly the result of an increasingly crowded speculative short, we would expect some normalization in positioning to remove pressure from the market. Instead, some shorts have already covered while yields remain near their highs.

That reinforces the conclusion from the previous chart. Oil and the Iran conflict have increasingly replaced labor surprises as an important marginal driver of rates, while the structural forces behind term premium remain intact. Persistent deficits, enormous Treasury financing requirements, inflation uncertainty, and geopolitical risk are determining the level investors require to own duration. Speculative positioning can accelerate that process, but it increasingly looks more like an amplifier than the underlying cause.

The distinction becomes particularly important because today's positioning creates significant asymmetry around the path of yields. With speculative shorts still historically large, any catalyst that pushes rates lower can produce an outsized rally as investors cover exposure. A decline in crude, meaningful progress surrounding Iran, a weak employment report, or softer inflation data could initially pull the 10-year lower and force shorts to cover. That buying can then push yields considerably farther than the original macro catalyst alone would justify.

A 15 to 20 basis point decline in yields should therefore not automatically be interpreted as evidence that the structural long-end problem has been resolved. With this much short exposure still embedded in Treasury futures, part of any sharp rally can simply represent positioning normalization. The more important test comes afterward.

If speculative shorts are materially reduced and the 10-year subsequently rebuilds toward the 4.8% to 5% area, the signal becomes considerably more consequential. It would suggest the market continues demanding those yields even after one of the major technical sources of selling has been removed. At that point, the argument increasingly shifts from positioning toward a structural clearing-price problem driven by inflation, fiscal supply, term premium, and insufficient demand for duration at lower yields.

The opposite outcome would also be informative. If crude rolls over, inflation expectations soften, shorts cover, and the 10-year establishes a sustainably lower range, it would suggest that a meaningful portion of the recent term-premium increase was tied to the geopolitical and commodity shock rather than a permanent repricing of U.S. sovereign duration. That would provide considerably more relief to housing and the other rate-sensitive portions of the economy than a simple Fed decision to leave the policy rate unchanged.

This is also where the Fed's increasingly hawkish reaction function becomes relevant. If oil remains elevated and policymakers continue signaling a willingness to hike, front-end shorts can remain supported while inflation uncertainty keeps pressure on the long end. But if the Fed ultimately tightens enough to establish greater inflation credibility, the curve could respond in a less intuitive way. The 2-year could remain elevated while longer yields stabilize or decline as investors reduce the inflation premium required farther out the curve.

For risk management, the distinction between level and path is therefore critical. The fundamental backdrop may justify elevated long-term yields while positioning makes the route toward that equilibrium extremely volatile. The Treasury market can experience violent rallies without entering a new bull market in duration, just as it can sell off sharply without every basis point representing a deterioration in fiscal fundamentals.

For now, the evidence increasingly argues that positioning is not the entire story. Shorts remain enormous, but some have already been covered while yields remain near their highs. Combined with the more than 60% rolling correlation between WTI and the 10-year discussed above, that strengthens the case that oil, inflation uncertainty, fiscal supply, and term premium are setting the underlying pressure on yields.

The short position is the fuel for a Treasury rally if the catalyst arrives. It is becoming less convincing as the explanation for why yields are this high in the first place.

Labor Inflation

The Wage Mechanism Is Cooling

From an underlying inflation perspective, the more structural components we monitor continue to look considerably more benign than the headline inflation data. Housing inflation continues normalizing, while the labor side of the inflation equation shows little evidence of a renewed wage spiral. That distinction matters because oil can push headline inflation materially higher and influence expectations relatively quickly, but a more persistent inflation regime normally requires those price pressures to migrate into wages and broader domestic costs. For now, that transmission remains difficult to find.

The latest JOLTS report reinforces that point. Job Openings increased modestly to 7.271 million in July, but June was revised down by 177K to 7.182 million, leaving the level of labor demand little changed relative to what investors thought they were looking at one month ago. The more important deterioration came from actual labor-market transactions. Hires fell by 278K to 5.054 million and the hiring rate declined from 3.4% to 3.2%. Outside of the pandemic collapse, a hiring rate this low has largely been associated with the slow jobless-recovery years following the Global Financial Crisis.

At the same time, layoffs remain remarkably subdued. The Layoffs and Discharges rate actually fell from 1.1% to 1.0%, near the bottom of its historical range, while the Quits Rate remains around 1.9%. This continues to describe the labor market as a low-hire, low-fire environment rather than one experiencing conventional recessionary deterioration. Businesses have become extremely reluctant to add workers, but they remain equally reluctant to reduce existing headcount. That is why unemployment can remain relatively contained even while workers increasingly describe finding another job as difficult.

The left side of the chart below shows why quits are particularly important for the inflation discussion. The Quits Rate has historically maintained a strong relationship with the Atlanta Fed Wage Growth Tracker because workers generally quit when outside opportunities are plentiful and competing employers are willing to pay more for their labor. The surge in quits toward 3% during 2021 and 2022 therefore coincided with the acceleration in wage growth toward 7%. As labor-market mobility subsequently collapsed, wage growth followed it lower. Today, quits sit near 1.9% while overall wage growth has moderated toward 3.8%.

That relationship gives us a useful framework for interpreting what comes next. A meaningful rebound in quits from here, particularly if accompanied by stronger hiring, would indicate that worker bargaining power is returning and would make wage inflation more important to the Fed's reaction function. A continued decline in quits from already normalized levels would send almost the opposite signal. At some point, falling quits stop being constructive disinflation and begin telling us that workers are unwilling to leave because alternative employment opportunities have disappeared.

The right side of the chart adds some nuance. Wage growth for job switchers has recently rebounded to roughly 4.4% compared with 3.6% for job stayers. Ordinarily, renewed acceleration among switchers could be interpreted as evidence that labor competition is returning. In the current environment, however, the broader mobility data do not confirm that signal. The hiring rate is falling, quits remain depressed, and openings per unemployed worker have declined to roughly 1.05 from 2.0 at the 2022 peak and below the 1.19 level that prevailed during 2019. A modest rebound in compensation for the relatively small group successfully changing jobs is therefore less concerning when fewer workers are actually able or willing to make that transition.

The composition of openings also remains important. Private Education and Health Services now represent more than 21% of total Job Openings, several percentage points above their pre-pandemic share. Meanwhile, Manufacturing provides one of the few cyclical counterpoints, with Durable Goods Manufacturing vacancies increasing by 76K. That fits with the broader bifurcation discussed throughout our work. Aggregate hiring is stagnant while the capital-intensive portions of the economy connected to equipment, electronics, infrastructure, and AI remain comparatively stronger.

This is why the current labor market is increasingly part of the disinflation process rather than the source of the inflation problem. Limited mobility reduces workers' ability to obtain competing offers, which in turn limits the wage pressure employers must absorb to retain employees. New research using ADP microdata also suggests that a substantial portion of workers experienced real wage declines during the inflationary period because nominal wage adjustment is sticky. Inflation effectively accomplished part of the real wage adjustment without requiring nominal compensation to fall. With quits near 1.9%, that bargaining mechanism remains weak.

The productivity data make the labor-cost picture even more constructive. Second-quarter Nonfarm Business Productivity increased 1.4% annualized and 2.2% year over year, while Unit Labor Costs increased only 1.2% annualized and 1.4% over the past four quarters. Wage growth by itself is not the relevant inflation variable. What matters to businesses is how much compensation rises relative to the amount of output each worker produces. If productivity improves alongside wages, companies can increase compensation without experiencing the same increase in unit production costs.

That leaves a relatively favorable labor-cost configuration:

Compensation remains positive. Productivity is improving. Unit Labor Cost inflation is only 1.4% year over year.

This is also why the current debate around AI and productivity is so important for both the Fed and the administration. If AI ultimately allows businesses to produce substantially more output with the same or fewer workers, stronger productivity can raise potential growth while containing unit labor costs. That would provide a pathway toward stronger real economic growth without recreating the wage-driven inflation pressures experienced earlier in the cycle.

The problem is timing. The productivity benefits may take years to diffuse through the broader economy, while the inflationary costs of building the infrastructure are occurring today. Data centers require enormous amounts of power, semiconductors, memory, electrical equipment, construction capacity, industrial machinery, and specialized labor before the economy receives the full productivity payoff. Several FOMC members have increasingly focused on exactly that sequencing problem. AI may ultimately be a positive supply shock, but the investment required to get there is currently behaving like a significant demand shock.

This brings us back to the Fed's September dilemma. The labor data provide very little evidence that wages are currently responsible for keeping inflation above target. Hiring is stagnant, quits are depressed, layoffs remain low, productivity is improving, and Unit Labor Costs are running at only 1.4%. The renewed inflation pressure discussed above is coming much more clearly through oil, geopolitical disruptions, tariffs, and selected AI-related capital inputs.

Another rate hike would therefore be landing on one of the least dynamic hiring environments of the past decade and a half in an attempt to contain inflation that is not primarily being generated by labor demand. That does not mean the Fed cannot hike. After more than five years above target, Warsh and several other FOMC members are increasingly focused on preserving inflation credibility rather than simply identifying the original source of each price shock. But it does mean the collateral cost of additional tightening is becoming more important.

The market reaction function remains caught between those two forces. Higher oil prices and persistent headline inflation reduce the probability of cuts and keep September tightening optionality alive. At the same time, stagnant hiring and benign Unit Labor Costs argue that the domestic wage mechanism is already doing much of the adjustment the Fed historically tries to create through tighter policy.

That leaves the barbell we have discussed increasingly dependent on the path of rates. If inflation moderates enough to remove tightening expectations, lower yields and a weaker dollar provide a powerful release valve for metals, Bitcoin, and other duration-sensitive assets. If oil continues higher and forces the Fed toward another hike, that relief is delayed even though the labor market itself is providing little justification for additional restraint.

For now, the message from JOLTS is relatively clear: the labor market is frozen, not breaking, and it is increasingly difficult to argue that wages are the source of today's inflation problem. The risk is that the Fed responds to inflation generated elsewhere by tightening into a labor market where the adjustment in hiring and worker mobility has already occurred.

Payroll Composition

The Headline Improved, the Breadth Still Matters

The August payroll report gave the Fed considerably more room to focus on the inflation side of its mandate. Nonfarm Payrolls increased by 162K, nearly three times the roughly 56K to 58K consensus estimate, while July was revised from a 23K decline to a 21K gain and June was revised higher from 20K to 31K. The Unemployment Rate remained at 4.1%, while the household survey was considerably stronger, with employment increasing by 569K and the labor force expanding by 683K. Participation improved two-tenths to 61.6%, U-6 unemployment declined to 7.7%, and the number of workers employed part time for economic reasons fell by 414K. After July raised legitimate questions about whether labor demand was beginning to break, August substantially reduced the immediate recessionary signal.

That matters for the September FOMC meeting because the labor side of the dual mandate had been the clearest argument for patience. The combination of weak July payrolls, falling hiring rates, low quits, and declining participation created a meaningful risk that additional tightening would land on an economy already moving toward a broader employment contraction. August does not reverse those structural concerns, but it gives policymakers greater latitude to prioritize inflation. With oil near $90, PCE still above target, and Kevin Warsh and other FOMC members increasingly emphasizing that inflation has remained elevated for too long, the hurdle for another hike has become lower now that the immediate employment downside looks less threatening.

The composition of the payroll gain, however, prevents us from interpreting the report as evidence of a broad hiring reacceleration. Roughly 101K jobs, or more than 60% of the entire increase, came from Restaurants and Local Government Education. ADP reported only 38K private payroll growth, Information employment continued declining, and the longer-term hiring trend remains historically weak. Average monthly payroll creation over the past twelve months is only around 31K. One strong month therefore improves the near-term distribution of outcomes without changing the broader labor regime.

The chart below makes that distinction clearer by stripping Health Care and Social Assistance out of payroll momentum. On a three-month average basis, headline Nonfarm Payroll growth has recovered to roughly 71K, while payroll growth excluding Health Care and Social Assistance is only around 45K. The gap is not enormous today, but the longer history shows how disproportionately important Health Care and Social Assistance have become in sustaining employment growth as hiring across the rest of the economy has slowed. This is particularly relevant because health-related employment tends to be less cyclically sensitive than Construction, Manufacturing, Professional Services, Information, or other areas more closely tied to changes in private-sector demand.

The broader message is therefore consistent with the JOLTS discussion above. The labor market is not breaking, but neither has it returned to a high-hire environment. Job Openings remain around 7.3 million, yet the Hiring Rate has fallen to 3.2%, the Quits Rate remains near 1.9%, and layoffs remain historically subdued. August payrolls fit within that low-hire, low-fire regime. Businesses are retaining existing workers while becoming increasingly selective about adding new ones.

The household survey nevertheless provided an important improvement relative to July. The increase in labor-force participation matters because recent stability in the Unemployment Rate had partly reflected people leaving the workforce. In August, labor supply moved back in the opposite direction. The labor force increased by 683K and employment increased by 569K while unemployment remained at 4.1%. That is a healthier configuration than an unchanged unemployment rate produced primarily through declining participation. It does not reverse the structural decline in participation discussed previously, but it removes one of the more concerning features of the July report.

Wages also remain relatively benign from an inflation perspective. Average Hourly Earnings increased 0.3% month over month but are up only 3.1% year over year. Combined with the Quits Rate near 1.9%, slowing hiring, improving productivity, and Unit Labor Costs increasing only 1.4% over the past year, there remains little evidence that labor is generating the current inflation problem. The employment report strengthened the growth side of the Fed's reaction function without materially worsening the wage side.

That distinction is important. A stronger labor report does not necessarily mean the Fed needs to suppress employment. It means policymakers have greater room to respond to inflation originating elsewhere without immediately fearing that another 25 basis points will trigger a firing cycle. With oil increasingly driving both inflation uncertainty and long-term Treasury yields, August payrolls effectively removed one of the strongest near-term constraints on a more hawkish Fed.

For markets, that explains why the report repriced September tightening probabilities rather than producing the straightforward "good news is good news" response associated with an early-cycle labor acceleration. Stronger employment reduces recession risk, which is constructive for earnings, but it simultaneously removes an important reason for the Fed to tolerate above-target inflation. With financial conditions already tightening through oil and long-term yields, that trade-off becomes increasingly important.

The correct interpretation is therefore narrower than the headline suggests. August substantially reduced the probability that the labor market is entering an imminent contraction, but it did not establish that broad-based hiring has restarted. Payroll growth remains concentrated, labor churn remains historically weak, and the longer-term trend remains close to stall speed.

Cyclical Labor Internals

Early Stabilization Is Showing Up Beneath the Headline

The composition of August payrolls was concentrated, but the cyclical details beneath the headline were more constructive than that concentration alone would suggest. Manufacturing added 16K jobs, Construction added 22K, Machinery Manufacturing added 6K, Fabricated Metal Products added another 6K, and Nonresidential Specialty Trade Contractors increased by 8K. Manufacturing employment has now risen by roughly 58K since December 2025, which fits with the improvement we have been tracking across ISM New Orders, regional Fed manufacturing surveys, capital spending intentions, and the broader AI-related infrastructure buildout. The labor market is not broadly reaccelerating, but several of the industries most sensitive to the industrial cycle are beginning to move in the right direction.

The BLS Employment Diffusion Index provides a useful way to distinguish those two statements. Rather than measuring the number of jobs created, the diffusion index measures the breadth of employment changes across industries. A reading above 50 means more industries are adding workers than cutting them. Both the one-month and three-month measures have moved back above that threshold, to 55.6 and 55.4 respectively. Hiring may therefore remain slow in aggregate, but the direction of employment growth is no longer being driven by an increasingly narrow group of industries. More industries are expanding payrolls than contracting them, even if the magnitude of those additions remains relatively modest.

That is an important distinction from the headline payroll discussion above. August's 162K gain was heavily influenced by Restaurants and Local Government Education, so we would not characterize the report as evidence of broad-based hiring strength. The diffusion data are making a more subtle point. Beneath the concentration in the number of jobs created, the direction of employment change across industries has begun improving. Manufacturing and Construction participating in that improvement is particularly encouraging because those sectors tend to carry more information about the underlying cyclical economy than relatively defensive hiring in Health Care or Government.

Temporary Help Services provide another constructive leading signal. Temporary employment has historically tended to turn before broader payroll growth because businesses frequently adjust contingent workers before making permanent hiring decisions. When demand begins deteriorating, temporary positions are relatively easy to eliminate without committing to permanent layoffs. When demand begins improving, the same logic works in reverse. Businesses uncertain about the durability of an increase in orders can add temporary workers before assuming the higher fixed cost associated with permanent employees.

That is why the second chart deserves attention. Temporary Help Payrolls have finally returned to positive year-over-year growth at roughly 1.5% after spending several years in contraction. The improvement has been gradual rather than explosive, but the direction matters. Temporary employment began deteriorating well before the broader labor market weakened during this cycle, and its stabilization now suggests businesses may be moving beyond the most defensive stage of labor management.

Combined with the diffusion data, the signal becomes more useful. More industries are adding jobs than cutting them, Temporary Help employment is growing again, Manufacturing employment has increased by 58K since December, and Construction continues adding workers. None of that contradicts the historically weak Hiring Rate or the concentration within August's headline payroll gain. Instead, it suggests that the labor market may be transitioning from a low-hire, low-fire stagnation toward an early stabilization in cyclical hiring.

We would want to see confirmation before calling this a genuine labor reacceleration. The Hiring Rate remains only 3.2%, the Quits Rate is 1.9%, and the three-month payroll trend excluding Health Care and Social Assistance remains modest. A sustained improvement would require Temporary Help to continue accelerating, employment diffusion to move farther above 50, and the gains in Manufacturing and Construction to broaden into other private industries.

For now, however, these are precisely the types of leading internals we would expect to improve before the headline labor data look obviously stronger. August removed much of the immediate downside risk from the employment story, while the two charts below suggest the cyclical undercurrents are becoming somewhat healthier as well.

Bottom Line

Resilience Gives the Fed Less Cover to Wait

The most important development this week was not simply that payrolls surprised higher or that yields continued rising. It was that the distribution of macro risks became more complicated. The immediate threat of a labor-market break has diminished at precisely the moment inflation and long-term financing costs are becoming more difficult for policymakers to ignore. That combination gives the Fed greater freedom to focus on price stability, but it also increases the possibility that monetary policy tightens into an economy where the labor adjustment has already occurred.

There are enough constructive labor internals to argue against becoming defensive on growth. Cyclical employment is improving at the margin, breadth has moved back into expansion, and Temporary Help has begun turning higher. But those developments are still early and coexist with historically weak labor churn. The next several reports will determine whether this represents the beginning of a genuine improvement in private hiring or simply stabilization at a low level.

The more consequential risk sits outside employment. If the geopolitical premium in oil continues pushing inflation uncertainty and long-term yields higher, the economy effectively receives two forms of tightening simultaneously. The bond market raises the cost of capital while the Fed becomes more willing to reinforce that restraint through the policy rate. That is a considerably different configuration from one where stronger payrolls simply reflect healthier growth.

This is why the direction of the 10-year may matter more than the September decision itself. A Fed hike accompanied by falling oil and declining term premium could ultimately prove less restrictive than an unchanged policy rate accompanied by another leg higher in crude and long yields. The market increasingly needs to distinguish the instrument the Fed controls from the financial conditions the economy actually experiences.

Treasury positioning adds another layer of complexity because the enormous short base leaves room for violent rallies if the macro catalyst changes. But a positioning-driven rally would not necessarily resolve the underlying issue. The more important test would come after shorts cover. If yields subsequently return toward their highs, the market would be confirming that the clearing price for duration has structurally moved higher rather than simply reflecting speculative pressure.

That leaves the fall centered on a relatively narrow set of questions. Can cyclical labor improvement broaden without reigniting wage pressure? Can inflation moderate despite the oil shock? And can long-term yields stabilize without requiring materially weaker growth to get there?

The answers will determine whether the current environment develops into a healthier reflationary expansion or a more difficult form of late-cycle tightening. For now, growth is proving resilient enough to withstand the pressure. The risk is that resilience gives policymakers and the bond market permission to keep applying it until something finally does not.

References

Federal Reserve Economic Data: 10-year Treasury yields, WTI crude oil, JOLTS quits rate, Atlanta Fed wage-growth tracker series, total nonfarm payrolls, health care and social assistance payrolls, temporary help services payrolls, and U.S. recession indicators.

CFTC public reporting data: legacy futures-only non-commercial Treasury futures positioning.
